title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The study used one hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with a shared‑initial generation semantics, a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and a Mininet emulator as a preregistered contamination check. Execution completed using 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task; preregistered cap = 400). Observed outcomes: every initial LLM candidate passed the deterministic validator in both conditions (baseline 200/200, GVR 200/200). The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because the baseline unsafe‑change incidence was 0%, the preregistered hypothesis (≥50% relative reduction) could not be meaningfully evaluated on this task bank. We report the frozen design, execution manifest, contingency counts, representative examples, and targeted discussion of operational implications and limitations grounded in archived artifacts (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent‑driven network configuration with generative models promises efficiency but raises safety risks: incorrect or unsafe configurations can cause outages, violate policies, or introduce vulnerabilities. Prior proposals combine LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to reduce such risks. Quantitative, preregistered evidence that a deterministic GVR pipeline materially lowers observable validator‑detected unsafe‑change incidence for representative NetOps tasks remains limited. We preregistered and ran study cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 to answer: does a deterministic GVR pipeline materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes compared to LLM‑only generation on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Our contributions: (1) a sealed paired preregistered design (n = 200); (2) a fully archived deterministic execution comparing LLM‑only and GVR under shared‑initial semantics; (3) transparent reporting of a null/negative confirmatory outcome with artifact‑grounded interpretation and threats to validity.
sections.related_work: LLMs show factual errors and prompt sensitivity; mitigation strategies include grounding (RAG), verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded agentic architectures. Prototype NetOps systems and intent→configuration workflows have shown feasibility but not production‑scale, fully instrumented failure‑rate characterization. Red‑team and configuration‑brittleness studies demonstrate that agentic tool descriptions, tool‑chaining, and persona/history can change safety outcomes. These prior results motivate preregistered, externally auditable evaluations that isolate whether adding deterministic repair materially reduces validator‑detected failure rates for a given model, prompt policy, and task bank.
sections.methodology: Preregistration: the sealed preregistration (study_id cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02) specified a paired confirmatory design (n = 200 tasks), primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), an exact McNemar two‑sided test (α = 0.05), and a model‑call cap (400). Task bank: a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks covering four topology clusters was used; tasks encode intent, initial and expected final states, and workflow constraints. Model and generation policy: a single hosted model, gpt‑5‑mini, was used with shared‑initial generation semantics (one initial generation per task reused for both baseline and guarded conditions). Deterministic/shared‑initial semantics were realized operationally by adapter‑enforced reuse of a single generated candidate per task: provider‑call and response artifacts show a single shared initial response file per task and identical baseline/guarded response files (see execution/responses/* files); the execution reconciliation records hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage 'shared_initial_generation' count = 200, i.e., one initial model call per task. The primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied full intent/constraint checks; a Mininet‑based emulator served as a preregistered secondary disagreement detector on a randomized holdout. Important preregistered analysis assumptions: a baseline unsafe‑change incidence ≈30% (power planning target) and a confirmatory target of ≥50% relative reduction. Analysis: primary test = exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired pass/fail outcomes; pre‑registered sensitivity analyses and exploratory secondary estimands included repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, and model‑call cost per successful repair.
sections.results: Execution completed successfully under the frozen plan (complete_pair_count = 200; model_calls_used = 200; maximum_model_calls = 400). Validation outcomes: every initial candidate passed the deterministic validator in both conditions — baseline 200/200, guarded 200/200. The observed 2×2 paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Confirmatory inference: paired difference estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed recorded in analysis artifact) = [0.0, 0.0]. Repair activity: because no initial candidate triggered a validator violation, no automated repair prompts were issued and all exploratory secondary estimands are vacuous for this execution. Contamination checks: the preregistered Mininet holdout produced no recorded validator–emulator disagreement flags in the contamination summary artifact. Determinism evidence: for representative tasks (e.g., task‑000001) the shared‑initial response file and the baseline/guarded response files are identical; execution reconciliation shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts indicating shared_initial_generation = 200, demonstrating adapter‑enforced single shared initial generations rather than independent model calls per condition.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and scope: the preregistered hypothesis that GVR would yield a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes is not supported on this curated task bank and deterministic execution because the baseline unsafe incidence was 0%. Practically, when the chosen prompts, model, shared‑initial policy, and validator coverage yield validator‑passing outputs for the target workload, an added automated repair step will not reduce validator‑detected failures. This null result should not be taken to invalidate GVR generally: three non‑exclusive explanations are artifact‑supported — (1) the model/prompts and shared‑initial policy produced candidates that already satisfied the validator constraints; (2) the primary deterministic validator enforces the specific intent constraints used to construct the task bank and therefore found no violations; (3) the task bank may be insufficiently adversarial or diverse to expose failure modes where repair helps. Limitations and reproducibility gaps (artifact‑grounded): (a) single‑model and shared‑initial setting — only gpt‑5‑mini under adapter‑enforced reuse was tested; outcomes may differ with other models, sampling temperatures, or independent calls per condition; (b) validator coverage — deterministic validators can omit vendor‑ or device‑level idiosyncrasies detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment; (c) adversarial robustness — the run did not include active red‑team injections; (d) preregistered holdout seed: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the emulator contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the public bundle, which prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection; the contamination summary artifact shows no disagreements but the missing seed is an archived‑bundle reproducibility gap that we report here. Operational implication: GVR's value is conditional — it can reduce validator‑detected failures when initial generation often violates validator constraints or when validator coverage is incomplete; a null result here highlights the need to measure baseline failure rates and validator coverage before deploying automated repairs. Future work: evaluate multiple model families, non‑zero temperature sampling regimes, adversarial task draws, broader device/vendor modeling, larger repair budgets, and human‑in‑the‑loop approval workflows.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic validator. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction is not supported on this task bank because the baseline failure rate was 0%. This null finding is narrowly scoped and underscores that empirical benefits of GVR depend on baseline error prevalence, model/prompts, validator coverage, and task hardness. Robust operational conclusions require multi‑model, adversarial, and emulator/real‑device evaluations beyond this single deterministic run.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02. LLM and orchestration: experiments used the hosted model declared as gpt-5-mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked through the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). The primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (Batfish‑style intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector on a randomized holdout. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n=200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run was performed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and artifact manifest entries are archived in the execution bundle (paths referenced in the manuscript point to the archived evidence). Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the emulator contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the public bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The initial master prompt reference above is the immutable archived master prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200). Results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and deterministic setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, sampling temperatures, or independent calls per condition.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

External validity: no production device flash deployment or long‑horizon rollout testing was performed; Mininet emulator disagreement checks were preregistered as contamination detectors but the missing holdout seed is a reproducibility gap for exact reconstruction of the selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
